transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-07-15 16:00 PDT | Duration: ~48m | Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood SRE) -- Svetlana (Head of ML), Rahul (Infra), Lina (ML Eng), Tom (Security)

Summary: quick technical review of quantization options for Pioneer Analytics models, focus on accuracy regressions and runtime perf.

00:00:00 Jordan: All right, everyone on? Good afternoon, thanks for joining, um this is Jordan from Redwood Inference, with Maya and Diego. we're gonna run through the quantization tradeoffs and then dig into the benchmarks you wanted.
00:00:15 Svetlana: Yep hi thanks, sorry for the slight delay, we had a quick sync. We're really interested in reducing GPU costs but can't accept meaningful accuracy loss for our extraction tasks.
00:00:28 Maya: Totally, that's the main tradeoff. We'll cover INT8, FP8, and the two post-training algorithms you mentioned -- GPTQ and AWQ -- and show how they behave on both throughput and the kinds of evals you care about.
00:00:42 Rahul: quick question, we run models in our VPC on GCP, and sometimes on-prem for regulated clients; how different will the deployment be with quantized kernels?
00:00:55 Diego: Good Q. From the infra side, quantized kernels are just different binaries / runtime builds; for Redwood Private we deliver the same runtime but you pick the quantization profile. On-prem it's more about having the compat lib for AVX/AMX or NVIDIA tensor cores. There may be a bit of tuning to get optimal batch sizes.
00:01:12 Lina: Are there concerns with KMS or data-in-transit when we move KV cache around for warm starts?
00:01:20 Tom: yeah security is our concern: does quantization affect logging or audit trails?
00:01:26 Maya: No, quantization doesn't change auditability. The KV cache is an in-memory structure and remains in your VPC. We do have options to encrypt caches at rest if you persist them to disk, and KMS integration is supported for keys.

00:02:05 Jordan: Okay let's start with the accuracy slide -- high level. INT8 is simple and fast but can have larger accuracy regressions on certain attention heads and norm layers. FP8 is more forgiving in some LLMs but requires hardware that supports FP8. GPTQ and AWQ are post-training quantization algorithms, GPTQ focuses on per-channel Hessian-aware rounding, AWQ uses activation-aware calibration and can be faster to compute.
00:02:30 Svetlana: We've run some small GPTQ tests and saw about 3% drop on our NER F1, which is borderline. We were hoping AWQ might be less regressive.
00:02:45 Maya: That matches community findings. AWQ often preserves accuracy a bit better for token classification, but results are model and task dependent. We'll run your prompts to see. Also important: combination approaches (FP8 for attention, INT8 for feedforward) sometimes hit a sweet spot.

00:03:10 Rahul: From perf side what kind of p95 latency differences are we looking at? We care about 99th percentile on short prompts (<=256 tokens).
00:03:20 Maya: For short prompts, INT8 on A100 or H100 can be 1.6x-2x faster per token vs FP16 depending on kernels and batch. FP8 can be comparable to FP16 or slightly faster depending on library support. But, and this is important, KV cache behavior matters: if you're doing many short requests with warm KV cache, the per-token compute often dominates so quantization helps more; if you have cold starts repeatedly, token generation must include cache warm-up costs.
00:03:47 Lina: Can you explain the KV cache interplay again? We use lots of few-shot contexts.
00:03:53 Maya: Sure. When you have a warm KV cache, the attention compute for the prefix is avoided and the decoder only attends to new tokens, so runtime per token is lower. But quantization can affect memory layout; AWQ/GPTQ kernels sometimes change memory access patterns and that can slightly change cache hit times, so it's worth including KV warm/cold scenarios in the benchmark.

00:04:25 Svetlana: What about batch sizes? We batch on the server side to improve throughput, but we need to keep tail latency low for interactive users.
00:04:33 Diego: There's a tradeoff: small batching (2-8) smooths GPU utilization with modest latency increases; large batching (16+) is great for throughput but hurts p99. Redwood's runtime supports latency SLO routing so you can route latency-sensitive requests to lower-batch workers or dedicated capacity.
00:04:50 Jordan: For this pilot we'll recommend two profiles: optimized for latency (small batch, KV warm, prioritized scheduling) and optimized for cost (aggressive batching, INT8 where acceptable).

00:05:12 Tom: On the security doc side, we need SOC2 and details about key management and audit logs.
00:05:18 Jordan: We'll attach our SOC2 summary and a short KMS integration guide. Diego, anything from the SRE side?
00:05:25 Diego: We'll also provide a VPC/on-prem checklist: required kernel modules, GPU driver minimums, and a matrix of runtime builds per quant format. That will make your on-prem rollout smoother.

00:06:00 Maya: Let's look at some numeric examples from our internal runs. Example: baseline FP16 p95 per-token latency for 512 context on an A100 was 8.4ms, INT8 tuned kernels came down to around 5.1ms per token, FP8 in our tests hovered at 6.9ms but had better perplexity preservation on some models.
00:06:28 Lina: those numbers are great. do you have throughput for batch=8?
00:06:34 Maya: For batch 8, FP16 sustained throughput was ~210 tokens/s, INT8 ~360 tokens/s, FP8 ~300 tokens/s. Again, model dependent; we'll run your exact weights.

00:07:00 Svetlana: Accuracy regressions: can you explain how we'll measure them beyond simple perplexity? Our NER pipeline is sensitive to entity boundary changes.
00:07:10 Maya: We'll run task-specific metrics: NER F1, QA exact match, and also proposed a custom eval set you provide. We'll give per-layer sensitivity analysis so you can see which layers contribute to regressions. Also, we can propose mixed precision: keep attention projection in FP16 and quantize FFN to INT8, often reduces regressions.

00:07:48 Rahul: For on-prem we worry about availability of tensor cores for FP8. If our fleet is diverse, is it okay to use mixed configs?
00:07:58 Diego: You can create node pools with specific runtime builds. Redwood Dedicated supports node labels, so latency-sensitive traffic goes to nodes with the FP8-compatible runtime, others to INT8-friendly nodes. There's also automated fallback when a node can't serve the requested quant profile.

00:08:20 Lina: Any licensing concerns with using GPTQ or AWQ code?
00:08:25 Maya: The algorithms are typically open source but check specific implementations. Redwood's runtime uses permissive libs and we maintain compatibility. We'll include notes about third-party licenses in the deliverable.

00:08:50 Svetlana: Let's talk about worst-case accuracy: what thresholds should we set for rollback? For us, NER F1 drop >1% is an immediate rollback.
00:08:58 Jordan: Makes sense. We'll show a canary rollout plan: start with small percentage traffic on quantized variant, monitor metrics (F1, latency, error rate), automatic rollback if thresholds exceeded.

00:09:18 Maya: Now specifics for your model: from what you shared in the quick assessment, it's a 7B decoder-only model with about 32 attention heads and pretty skewed token distribution. That shape often shows more sensitivity in the FFN when quantized.
00:09:32 Lina: yes, we see FFN-sensitive regressions.

00:09:40 Maya: For that topology we'll likely try two experiments: 1) GPTQ per-channel on feedforward with 8-bit activation quantization and FP16 attention; 2) AWQ across whole model but with a higher precision calibration and layer re-ordering. We'll compare accuracy and perf.

00:10:05 Svetlana: How long will these experiments take to run? We need results quickly to decide on contract renewal.
00:10:12 Maya: For a 7B model, a full sweep with your eval set (5k samples) plus perf tests on 2xA100 should be doable in 24-48 hours of compute. We'll prioritize and aim to deliver results by 2026-07-20.

00:10:35 RahuI: (sic) Sorry Rahul: Our infra wants to know GPU hours estimate and if you need a dedicated slot.
00:10:42 Maya: We'll need about 8-12 GPU hours on A100 per algorithm variant; if you want parallel runs we can request a dedicated slot. Jordan: will this be covered by the pilot credit?
00:10:52 Jordan: Yes we'll include it in the pilot scope, no extra charge for the first benchmark run.

00:11:10 Tom: A question on telemetry: will quantized runs still produce the same trace ids and call metadata so we can compare across variants?
00:11:18 Diego: Yes, trace ids and request metadata are unchanged; only the runtime kernel differs. We'll surface per-request token costs and latency in the console.

00:11:40 Svetlana: In prior tests we saw occasional hallucination increases post-quantization. Do you typically see that?
00:11:47 Maya: Hallucinations can increase if the model distribution shifts, especially on open-ended tasks. On constrained generation (NER) it's less common but possible. We'll include generation-based QA checks in the eval. If hallucination increases we'll look at mixing precision or re-calibrating certain layers.

00:12:12 Lina: Do you support dynamic quantization at runtime? Like switching between INT8 and FP16 per request?
00:12:20 Diego: Redwood supports model variants and routing by policy. You can expose both the FP16 and quantized variant and route by header, user tier, or latency SLO. Switching per-request is effectively routing to different deployment variants.

00:12:44 Maya: Ok let's sketch the benchmark plan: tasks: run accuracy eval (NER F1) on your eval set, run throughput/latency sweep (batch 1..16, KV warm and cold), run per-layer sensitivity, and compute cost-per-token delta. We'll produce a spreadsheet and a recommendations doc.

00:13:05 Svetlana: Sounds good. For KV warm/cold, please include few-shot contexts we use in production, around 5-shot examples.

00:13:18 Jordan: Noted. We'll request the prompt set. Any other infra constraints?
00:13:24 Rahul: We use strict egress policies; will Redwood need egress to run these benchmarks?
00:13:30 Jordan: For Redwood-managed benchmark we run in our infra, but for Private/on-prem we'll run the code you provide inside your VPC. For the first pass we'll run in Redwood's sandbox unless you prefer otherwise.

00:13:52 Tom: For compliance, we might prefer the on-prem run; we'll decide after we see the first results.

00:14:00 Maya: Ok, last technical note: GPTQ can be slow to quantize (hours for larger models) because it solves per-channel approximations; AWQ is often faster to apply but may require more calibration data. We'll log wall time for each approach.

00:14:20 Lina: Are there fallback options if a quantized variant regresses in the wild?
00:14:24 Jordan: yes canary rollouts + instant rollback + auto-fallback to FP16 or another compatible variant. Redwood also supports automatic rollback based on metric thresholds.

00:14:40 Svetlana: Great, that addresses our operational concerns.

00:14:48 Jordan: Recap of next steps: Pioneer shares prompts and eval set by 2026-07-17, Redwood runs GPTQ/AWQ/INT8 benchmarks and returns spreadsheet + writeup by 2026-07-20, Redwood sends SOC2 summary and KMS notes, and we schedule a 30m follow-up on 2026-07-22.
00:15:05 Lina: perfect.

00:15:12 Jordan: Anything else before we wrap?
00:15:15 Svetlana: No that's it. Thanks everyone.
00:15:20 Jordan: Thanks, we'll follow up in the notes and send the action items. Appreciate your time.

[End of transcript - approximate timestamps omitted after 15:20 but conversation continued with logistical chat and calendar invites for ~30 minutes total. Transcript includes minor transcription artifacts like 'RahuI' and occasional mis-heard model names.]
